column3: Does every irreducible reversible discrete-time Markov chain on \(n\ge2\) states satisfy \(\mathbb E_{\pi}C\ge(n-1)H_{n-1}\), where the initial state has stationary distribution \(\pi\), \(C\) counts transitions until every state has been visited, and \(H_j=\sum_{i=1}^{j}1/i\)?
column4: An exact extremal bound would identify how quickly a reversible exploration process can cover its state space.
column5: Check subsequent literature and record the conventions for cover time and chains with self-loops against Aldous–Fill, Open Problem 6.30.

column3: Does Swendsen–Wang dynamics for the zero-field ferromagnetic four-state Potts model on the \(L\times L\) square torus at critical temperature have worst-case total-variation mixing time polynomial in \(L\), counting a full cluster update as one step?
column4: This isolates the unresolved critical sampling threshold between established polynomial and quasipolynomial guarantees.
column5: Write the transition kernel, critical inverse temperature and mixing threshold explicitly; verify the transfer between spectral-gap and mixing bounds.

column3: Determine the asymptotic inverse spectral gap of Swendsen–Wang dynamics for the zero-field critical Ising model on the \(L\times L\) square torus; in particular, decide whether it is \(L^{z+o(1)}\) and determine the exponent \(z\).
column4: The dynamic critical exponent measures the intrinsic cost of cluster sampling near a phase transition.
column5: Specify the kernel and Ising normalization; decide how to express the target if the exponent limit does not exist. Numerical estimates do not certify the exponent.

column3: Does Wang–Swendsen–Kotecký dynamics mix in polynomial time on every \(n\)-vertex graph of maximum degree \(\Delta\) with \(q\ge\Delta+1\) colors, when a step chooses two distinct colors and independently swaps them on each induced connected component with probability \(1/2\)?
column4: A sharp general-graph guarantee would establish when cluster updates overcome barriers facing single-vertex coloring samplers.
column5: Specify uniform dependence on both \(n\) and \(q\), the stationary law and total-variation threshold; confirm irreducibility in the complete stated range.

column3: Does Wang–Swendsen–Kotecký dynamics on proper three-colorings of the \(N\times N\) square torus, for even \(N\), have polynomial worst-case total-variation mixing time?
column4: This tests whether cluster sampling remains efficient at a canonical antiferromagnetic critical point.
column5: Define the periodic graph and color-swap kernel, prove the relevant state-space connectivity, and specify the mixing threshold.

column3: Determine the uniqueness and phase-coexistence regimes of the hard-core model on \(\mathbb Z^2\) as the activity \(\lambda>0\) varies, including whether a single sharp critical activity separates them.
column4: The lattice transition organizes the behavior of independent-set sampling and spatial correlations.
column5: Define infinite-volume Gibbs measures and boundary conditions; separate existence of a sharp threshold from numerical localization of it and specify the acceptance domain.

column3: Can an exactly uniform random spanning tree of every connected unweighted undirected graph be generated in expected \(O(m)\) time in the word-RAM model, where \(m\) is the number of edges?
column4: This asks whether exact random generation can match the cost of reading the graph.
column5: Specify the input representation, word size, random-bit operations and whether preprocessing is included; verify exact rather than approximate uniformity.

column3: For a connected undirected graph \(G\) and \(k\) independent lazy random walks with worst-case starting vertices, characterize within constant factors the expected time until their union visits every vertex.
column4: A graph-general cover-time law would quantify the speedup obtainable from parallel random exploration.
column5: Specify the admissible characterization, the range of \(k\), laziness, and whether the worst case ranges over all starting tuples or a common starting vertex.

column3: Is there an ordering of all spanning trees of \(K_n\) in which consecutive trees exchange one edge and both ranking a tree and recovering a tree from its rank take time polynomial in \(n\)?
column4: This combines minimal-change generation with efficient random access to a fundamental combinatorial family.
column5: Specify the tree encoding, binary ranks, endpoints versus cyclic adjacency, and uniform complexity of the ordering.

column3: Does every finite connected undirected graph admit a listing of all its spanning trees exactly once in which each transition deletes and inserts edges sharing an endpoint?
column4: A pivot-exchange ordering would impose a much stronger locality condition than ordinary edge-exchange enumeration.
column5: Define the allowed graph class and list endpoints; the source asks for existence, without a cyclic requirement or an efficient generation guarantee.

column3: For every finite directed graph and fixed root with at least one spanning out-arborescence, can all spanning out-arborescences be listed exactly once so that successive members exchange one arc?
column4: This extends minimal-change enumeration to rooted directed connectivity and implies the undirected pivot-exchange existence statement.
column5: Specify loops and parallel arcs and whether the root is part of the input; require a path through all arborescences, not a Hamilton cycle.

column3: For \(n\ge2k+1\), excluding \((n,k)=(5,2)\), is there a uniform algorithm generating a cyclic ordering of all \(k\)-subsets of \([n]\) with consecutive sets disjoint and polynomial delay in \(n\) and \(k\)?
column4: The question separates existence of a combinatorial Gray cycle from its efficient generation.
column5: Specify preprocessing, workspace, output encoding and the delay across the final-to-first transition; retain the source's exceptional pair.

column3: Can the number of subsets of \(n\) nonnegative integer weights with sum at most a given capacity be approximated within relative error \(\varepsilon\), with constant success probability, in \(\widetilde O(n\,\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon))\) time?
column4: An input-linear approximate counter would sharpen the complexity of a basic counting problem beyond decision and optimization.
column5: Specify binary input lengths, arithmetic operations, hidden logarithms and success probability; compare the cited October 2026 improvement before certifying openness.

column3: In centrally \(\varepsilon\)-differentially private \(K\)-armed bandits against an oblivious adversary, can expected regret be bounded by the nonprivate \(O(\sqrt{KT})\) term plus a privacy penalty independent of the horizon \(T\), apart from logarithmic factors?
column4: This asks whether privacy adds a separate cost or fundamentally multiplies the difficulty of adversarial learning.
column5: Specify neighboring loss sequences, the public transcript, admissible privacy penalty as a function of \(K,\varepsilon\), loss range and hidden logarithms.

column3: Determine the optimal sample complexity of polynomial-time \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-private algorithms finding approximate Goldstein-stationary points of Lipschitz nonsmooth nonconvex population losses with bounded initial suboptimality.
column4: The tradeoff connects privacy, statistical sample size and a general notion of stationarity beyond smooth optimization.
column5: Define Goldstein stationarity, neighborhood radius, error, loss oracle, failure probability, normalization and matching-bound precision.

column3: Determine the query complexity of distinguishing Boolean functions on \(\{0,1\}^n\) that are \(\varepsilon_1\)-close to monotone from those \(\varepsilon_2\)-far, for fixed \(0<\varepsilon_1<\varepsilon_2<1\).
column4: Tolerance changes monotonicity testing from detecting defects to estimating distance, exposing a large unexplained query gap.
column5: Fix uniform Hamming distance, success probability and adaptive versus nonadaptive access; these are separate complexity functions and must not be conflated.

column3: Given membership-query access to a measurable set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), can convexity versus constant Gaussian-measure distance from every convex set be tested with polynomially many queries in \(n\)?
column4: This asks whether a basic high-dimensional geometric property is accessible through a small black-box interface.
column5: Fix the distance constant, one-sided versus two-sided error, random sampling access and the representation of real query points.

column3: With adaptive random access to a length-\(n\) array, can the length of its longest increasing subsequence be estimated within additive error \(\varepsilon n\) in time polynomial in \(\log n\) and \(1/\varepsilon\)?
column4: This tests whether global order can be estimated with efficient dependence on both input length and accuracy.
column5: Specify the value universe, strict versus weak subsequences, success probability and query versus total running time; keep adaptivity explicit.

column3: For \(n\times n\) matrices over \(\mathbb F_2\) with bounded row and column sparsity, determine the row/column adjacency-query complexity of estimating rank within additive error \(\varepsilon n\).
column4: Rank estimation tests whether a global algebraic invariant can be recovered from local sparse access.
column5: Fix the degree bound, adjacency-query interface and success probability; distinguish the source's conjectured linear lower bound from a full complexity characterization.

column3: For independent \(\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) costs \(C_{i,j,k}\), is there a polynomial-time algorithm choosing permutations \(\pi,\sigma\) with \(\sum_i C_{i,\pi(i),\sigma(i)}\le(1+o(1))\operatorname{OPT}\) with high probability as \(n\to\infty\)?
column4: Random multidimensional assignment is a canonical test of how distributional structure changes optimization complexity.
column5: Specify real-input arithmetic and probability conventions, the rate of the error term and the dimensions; finite-precision inputs need a separate justified model.

column3: When each directed edge of a complete graph has an independent uniform \([0,1]\) cost, can a minimum-cost Hamiltonian cycle be found exactly in polynomial time with high probability?
column4: This asks whether random instances remove the worst-case obstacle to exact asymmetric traveling-salesman optimization.
column5: Specify the arithmetic model, failure behavior, runtime guarantee and meaning of exact computation with continuously distributed costs.

column3: Determine the asymptotic worst-case expected approximation ratio of Best Fit bin packing when an adversary chooses the item multiset and its arrival order is uniformly random.
column4: The target measures how much a random arrival order improves a classical greedy packing rule.
column5: Define the asymptotic supremum over instances, tie breaking and additive terms; the default numerical benchmark tolerance is distinct from exact identification of the ratio.

column3: Is there a deterministic increment sequence depending only on \(n\) for which standard Shellsort uses \(O(n\log n)\) expected comparisons on a uniformly random permutation of \(n\) keys?
column4: This would determine whether the original increment-based sorting method can be average-case optimal.
column5: Specify valid increments and insertion-sort costs within each residue class; randomized Shellsort and other sorting procedures are different algorithms.

column3: For each fixed dimension \(d\), can an outer approximation \(P\) with \(K\subseteq P\subseteq K+\varepsilon B\) be constructed efficiently using at most a dimension-dependent constant times the minimum feasible number of facets for that input \(K\) and error \(\varepsilon\)?
column4: Instance-optimal approximation would adapt representation size to the geometry of the particular polytope.
column5: Specify the input representation, scale normalization, the meaning of efficient construction and whether the optimum ranges over all outer polytopes.

column3: Is there an explicit dynamic Boolean data-structure problem with \(O(\log n)\)-bit operation arguments for which every polynomial-space adaptive cell-probe structure with \(\Theta(\log n)\)-bit cells needs \(n^{\Omega(1)}\) amortized update or query time, including bounded-error randomized structures?
column4: A polynomial unconditional barrier would change the known limits of dynamic data structures beyond polylogarithmic lower bounds.
column5: Define explicitness, admissible operation sequences, preprocessing, the error convention and the quantified update/query tradeoff.

column3: For the basic MultiQueue with \(q\) internal queues, uniformly random insertions and deletion of the smaller minimum from two random queues, determine the worst-case expected rank error over oblivious operation and key sequences, including insertions below previously deleted keys.
column4: This asks how relaxed priority queues behave without favorable assumptions about the order of priorities.
column5: Specify empty-queue behavior, concurrency or sequential semantics, rank ties and whether the error is per deletion or averaged over a sequence.

column3: For two-choice cuckoo hashing with bucket capacity \(b\), determine whether insertion time can be bounded independently of table size at every fixed load below the orientability threshold, with explicit dependence on the gap to that threshold.
column4: This isolates the algorithmic gap between feasible hash-table load and efficient insertion.
column5: Fix the hashing distribution, insertion rule, expected versus amortized cost and failure/rebuilding convention; check the parameter range of the July 2026 result.

column3: Starting from any binary search tree on \(n\) keys, does splaying the keys in the preorder sequence of any other binary search tree on the same keys take \(O(n)\) total time?
column4: The traversal conjecture is a classical structured-access barrier within the broader dynamic-optimality program.
column5: Specify the standard Splay operation and cost model; record that dynamic optimality implies this special case, while the converse is not asserted.

column3: Can exact breadth-first distances in an arbitrary undirected graph be computed in \(O(\operatorname{Sort}(n+m))\) I/Os even when its vertices do not fit in internal memory, where \(\operatorname{Sort}(N)=\Theta((N/B)\max\{1,\log_{M/B}(N/B)\})\)?
column4: This asks whether graph traversal can match the basic external-memory sorting bound.
column5: Specify the indivisible-record model, parameter range for \(M,B\), graph representation, output cost and source vertex.

column3: Can exact single-source shortest paths in an arbitrary undirected graph with nonnegative weights be computed in \(O(\operatorname{Sort}(n+m))\) I/Os without a bound on the edge-weight ratio or a semi-external memory assumption?
column4: The problem tests whether weighted graph exploration can be performed at sorting cost on external storage.
column5: Define the sorting bound, machine and weight representation, memory parameters and required distance/path output.

column3: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm constructing an optimal generalized binary split tree for given successful-query probabilities, where each node first tests equality to one key and otherwise branches using a potentially different split key?
column4: This identifies the complexity of a basic comparison-search model whose formerly claimed polynomial algorithm was invalid.
column5: Define the legal tree structure, successful-query costs, probability encoding and the role of empty branches; retain the distinction from ordinary optimal search trees.

column3: For positively weighted undirected graphs and integer \(k\ge2\), can a path-reporting distance oracle simultaneously use \(O(n^{1+1/k})\) space, have stretch \(2k-1\), and answer in constant overhead plus time proportional to the reported path?
column4: This asks whether compact distance summaries can return actual routes without losing their best size and stretch guarantees.
column5: Specify dependence on \(k\), word size, preprocessing, randomization and whether output cost counts edges or vertices.

column3: For every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), can an undirected nonnegatively weighted graph with \(m=O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) edges be preprocessed in \(O(n^{2-\delta})\) time for some \(\delta>0\) into a stretch-three distance oracle with \(O(n^{3/2})\) space and constant query time?
column4: The remaining stretch-three case tests whether compact distance oracles can be built genuinely faster than quadratic time on sparse inputs.
column5: Specify the weight and machine model, permitted randomization and the dependence of \(\delta\) on \(\varepsilon\).

column3: Can exact distances in a directed weighted graph with no negative cycles be maintained under insertion or deletion of a vertex and its incident edges using deterministic \(\widetilde O(n^{5/2})\) worst-case update time, \(\widetilde O(n^2)\) space and constant query time?
column4: This isolates the cost of removing randomness from a central worst-case dynamic shortest-path bound.
column5: Specify the maximum vertex universe, arithmetic model, initialization and treatment of supplied incident edges; do not confuse vertex updates with amortized single-edge targets.

column3: Can two-edge-connectivity queries in a fully dynamic undirected graph be supported with deterministic polylogarithmic worst-case time for both edge updates and queries?
column4: This asks whether resilience to one edge failure can be maintained without expensive occasional rebuilds.
column5: Define the query precisely, graph representation, preprocessing, word size and whether the structure reports bridges or only answers pair queries.

column3: Can a constant-factor approximation to edit distance between two strings be maintained under arbitrary single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions in polylogarithmic expected amortized update time after polynomial preprocessing?
column4: This would make a fundamental sequence-distance estimate efficiently maintainable throughout an evolving input.
column5: Specify alphabet, adversary, approximation guarantee, query time, space and probability conventions; the source records an editorial strengthening.

column3: For graphs whose rank-width always remains at most \(k\), can an implicit rank-decomposition of width \(O(k)\) be maintained under edge updates in \(f(k)\operatorname{polylog}n\) amortized time?
column4: This asks whether a structural graph parameter supports genuinely polylogarithmic dynamic maintenance.
column5: Define the decomposition interface, promise violations, randomness, preprocessing and constants hidden in its width and update bounds.

column3: Under edge updates preserving treewidth at most \(k\), can every fixed counting monadic second-order graph property be maintained in \(f(k,\varphi)\operatorname{polylog}n\) worst-case update time?
column4: A worst-case dynamic Courcelle theorem would make logical tractability stable under every individual update.
column5: Specify CMSO with edge-set quantification, the update promise, initialization, query time and the distinction from known amortized bounds.

column3: Can a deterministic structure decide planarity after arbitrary edge insertions and deletions in polylogarithmic worst-case time per operation?
column4: This asks whether dynamic topological feasibility can avoid all occasional expensive updates.
column5: Specify whether nonplanar intermediate graphs are allowed, the query/output interface, preprocessing and space.

column3: Can the exact arboricity value of a fully dynamic undirected graph be maintained in polylogarithmic amortized time per edge update with constant-time value queries?
column4: Value-only maintenance separates the intrinsic difficulty of arboricity from the cost of explicitly changing a forest decomposition.
column5: Specify word-RAM conventions, randomization, initialization and the input graph class; do not transfer lower bounds for explicit decompositions without justification.

column3: For an \(N\)-vertex directed grid with east, north and northeast arcs and nonnegative weights, can opposite-corner distance be maintained within \(1+\varepsilon\) using \(\operatorname{polylog}(N)\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon)\) update time and \(\sqrt N\operatorname{polylog}(N)\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon)\) query time, with polynomial preprocessing and an offline-known update sequence?
column4: The proposed tradeoff connects dynamic geometric distances to faster approximate time-series alignment.
column5: Specify grid shape, weight encodings, amortization, what offline knowledge is available and how all preprocessing costs depend on sequence length.

column3: Can planar halfplane constraints be inserted and deleted while maintaining a point minimizing a fixed linear objective subject to at most \(k\) violations, in \(k^{O(1)}\operatorname{polylog}n\) amortized update time and near-linear-plus-polynomial-in-\(k\) space?
column4: This asks whether robust optimization can support arbitrary deletions without advance lifetime information.
column5: Specify infeasibility and unboundedness, query time, real arithmetic, preprocessing and the exact space bound; the target strengthens a semi-online result.

column3: Can a randomized structure maintain a proper \((\Delta+1)\)-vertex coloring with constant-time color queries and polylogarithmic expected amortized edge-update time against an adaptive adversary, for graphs of maximum degree at most the supplied bound \(\Delta\)?
column4: Adaptive robustness is a central obstacle to making very fast randomized dynamic colorings reliable in interactive use.
column5: Specify what the adversary observes, correctness probability, initialization, recoloring interface and dependence on \(\Delta\).

column3: Can a fixed-alphabet text be maintained in \(O(n)\) words with polylogarithmic amortized time per character insertion or deletion and \(O(m+\mathrm{occ})\) worst-case time to report all occurrences of a queried length-\(m\) pattern?
column4: This seeks an optimal reporting interface that survives arbitrary edits throughout a text.
column5: Specify word size, current versus maximum text length, preprocessing, randomization and output positions; append-only or immediately reversed edits are weaker models.

column3: Can planar point insertions and deletions and queries for the intersections of a line with their convex hull all be supported in \(O(\log n)\) time using linear space, allowing amortized updates but requiring worst-case query time?
column4: The line-intersection interface asks for geometric information not covered by optimal extreme-point query bounds.
column5: Specify degenerate intersections, arithmetic model and output encoding; distinguish this query from the existing extreme-point convex-hull card.

column3: Can directed reachability be maintained under single-edge insertions and deletions by quantifier-free update formulas using finitely many auxiliary relations of arbitrary fixed arity?
column4: This tests the expressive power of quantifier-free dynamic computation beyond known bounded-arity lower bounds.
column5: Specify initialization, built-in relations and whether the query is all-pairs or designated-source reachability; use the exact DynProp model of the source.

column3: Is there a polynomial-time Boolean query on finite relational structures that cannot be maintained by first-order update formulas under single-tuple insertions and deletions, with arbitrary fixed-arity auxiliary relations and built-in arithmetic?
column4: An unconditional separation would establish a basic expressive limit of dynamic descriptive complexity.
column5: Specify empty-input initialization, auxiliary initialization, uniformity and the allowed arithmetic relations before asserting a separation.

column3: For every fixed \(\Delta\), is integer linear programming \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\le b,\ x\in\mathbb Z^n\}\) polynomial-time solvable when all square subdeterminants of the integer matrix \(A\) have absolute value at most \(\Delta\)?
column4: This asks whether a bounded departure from total unimodularity guarantees tractable integer optimization.
column5: Specify binary encoding, fixed-parameter dependence and infeasible/unbounded outcomes; retain zero determinants and unrestricted row sparsity.

column3: Is the lattice width of every convex body in \(\mathbb R^n\) whose interior contains no integer point at most \(Cn\), for one universal constant \(C\)?
column4: A linear flatness theorem would sharpen a foundational geometric limitation used in integer optimization.
column5: Define convex bodies and lattice width completely, distinguish empty interior from interior lattice-freeness, and check later improvements to the near-linear bound.

column3: For each fixed dimension \(d\ge3\), does the split closure of every rational polyhedron have an inequality description of size polynomial in the binary length of its input description?
column4: This asks whether a standard cutting-plane closure retains a compact representation in fixed dimension.
column5: Define the split-closure operation rather than just its disjunctions; specify whether size counts inequalities, coefficient bits, or both.

column3: For a convex body \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+d}\) with finite positive mixed-integer volume, is there a point in \(C\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)\) such that every closed halfspace containing it captures at least \(1/(2^n e)\) of that volume?
column4: A universal mixed-integer centerpoint guarantee would link convex geometry to progress bounds for cutting-plane optimization.
column5: Define the fiber-summed measure, dimension ranges and measurability; check the proposed constant and unrestricted versus thickness-qualified versions.

column3: Can one construct an explicit family of matroids on \(n\) elements whose base polytopes have linear extension complexity \(2^{\Omega(n)}\)?
column4: This asks for concrete exponential extension-complexity obstructions where counting already proves existence.
column5: Specify the representation and resource bound meant by explicit, whether rank-oracle access suffices, and the asymptotic family indexing.

column3: Does every minimum-knapsack covering instance admit an objective-independent extended linear relaxation of polynomial size with one universal constant integrality gap for all nonnegative cost vectors?
column4: This separates efficient approximate optimization from the existence of a uniformly compact relaxation.
column5: Define the covering instances, projection, encoding-length measure and treatment of zero optima; confirm that the target is polynomial rather than quasipolynomial size.

column3: Can maximum zero-one knapsack admit an objective-independent extended linear relaxation of size polynomial in \(n\) and \(1/\varepsilon\), with gap at most \(1+\varepsilon\) simultaneously for every nonnegative profit vector?
column4: A fully polynomial formulation scheme would provide one compact geometric certificate for all objectives.
column5: Specify coefficient-bit complexity, the gap convention and input dependence; distinguish a fixed-accuracy polynomial-size scheme from joint polynomial dependence.

column3: Can a connected weighted graph Laplacian system \(Lx=b\), with \(\sum_i b_i=0\), be solved to relative error \(1/10\) in the energy norm using expected \(O(m)\) arithmetic operations?
column4: This asks whether approximate Laplacian solving can reach literal input-linear arithmetic complexity.
column5: Define the energy-norm reference solution, success probability, arithmetic and random-bit operations, and weight assumptions; do not substitute bit complexity.

column3: Can the volume of an \(n\)-dimensional convex body be estimated to fixed relative accuracy with success probability at least \(2/3\) using \(O(n^2\operatorname{polylog}n)\) membership queries, given concentric inner and outer balls with polynomial radius ratio?
column4: This targets the dimension dependence of a fundamental randomized integration problem.
column5: Specify the fixed accuracy, oracle, rounding promises, arithmetic costs and radius-ratio dependence; query and total computation bounds are different.

column3: For every ideal clutter and every nonnegative integral capacity vector, does the dual covering linear program have an optimal packing with dyadic-rational coordinates?
column4: The conjecture asks whether integral covering geometry forces a special arithmetic form of optimal fractional packing.
column5: Define clutters, idealness, the primal-dual pair and dyadic denominators; check the scope of recent dijoin and local-dyadic results.

column3: Are the only minimally nonideal binary clutters the Fano-line clutter, the odd-circuit clutter of \(K_5\), and the clutter of complements of cuts of \(K_5\)?
column4: A forbidden-minor characterization would explain integrality across a central class of covering problems.
column5: Define binary clutters, minors and the three obstructions explicitly. The supplied text calls the third obstruction a blocker; the author's statement instead uses complements of cuts, which is the formulation retained here.

column3: Is every order automorphism of the partially ordered set of computably enumerable Turing degrees the identity?
column4: Rigidity would say that the reducibility position of a computably enumerable degree determines the degree itself.
column5: Define computably enumerable degrees and their pure order; distinguish this structure from all Turing degrees and document the relationship to biinterpretability.

column3: Is the universal-existential fragment of the first-order theory of computably enumerable Turing degrees decidable in the language containing only their ordering relation?
column4: This locates an important decidability boundary below the known undecidability of the full theory.
column5: Specify prenex blocks, equality and sentence encoding; adding join or meet symbols changes the question.

column3: For every finite \(n\ge1\), does every countable Boolean algebra with a low-\(n\) presentation also have a computable presentation, where low-\(n\) means that its atomic diagram has \(n\)-th jump equivalent to \(\emptyset^{(n)}\)?
column4: This tests whether a weak noncomputable presentation of an algebra can always be replaced by a computable one.
column5: Specify the presentation language and atomic-diagram coding; verify the exact range of the established small-\(n\) cases.

column3: For every coinfinite computably enumerable low-two set \(A\), is the lattice of its computably enumerable supersets modulo finite difference isomorphic to the lattice of all computably enumerable sets modulo finite difference?
column4: The question connects computational weakness of a set to the global structure of its supersets.
column5: Define the quotient lattice and low-two condition explicitly; retain the source's warning that earlier proof claims do not establish the general statement.

column3: Can arithmetic be interpreted in the pure order of computably enumerable Turing degrees with a definable coding map that assigns each degree an index for a computably enumerable set of that same degree?
column4: Full biinterpretability would recover individual computability degrees from order-theoretic information.
column5: Recover the precise coding-map and parameter conventions from the source; distinguish recovery of degrees from the established double-jump version.

column3: Is there an algorithm deciding which finite lattices embed into the computably enumerable Turing degrees while preserving joins and meets?
column4: This asks for an effective description of the finite algebraic patterns realizable by relative computability.
column5: Specify bounds and constants preserved by an embedding and how meet preservation is interpreted when meets need not exist globally.

column3: Is the universal-existential first-order theory of the \(\Sigma^0_2\) enumeration degrees decidable in the pure partial-order language?
column4: The target would identify the complexity of a low-quantifier theory of a fundamental reducibility structure.
column5: Define local enumeration degrees, the reducibility relation and quantifier fragment; verify the exact structure addressed by the Ahmad-pair source.

column3: Characterize using the constructible hierarchy the sets of reals decidable by infinite-time Turing machines with a countable uniform bound on halting times, together with the corresponding semidecidable classes.
column4: The problem asks which sets can be recognized with transfinite time budgets, beyond merely locating time suprema.
column5: Specify the machine's limit rule, parameter allowance and admissible form of a characterization; split decision and semidecision targets if the source requires distinct answers.

column3: Must every ordinal beginning a gap in attainable countable infinite-time decision times or semidecision times be admissible?
column4: A positive theorem would connect gaps in computational time spectra to the structure of admissible set theory.
column5: Define a gap, least uniform time and admissibility; keep the decision and semidecision versions distinct from clockable-ordinal results.

column3: Is every countable Borel equivalence relation Borel reducible to recursive isomorphism on \(2^\omega\), where sequences are equivalent when one is obtained from the other by a computable permutation of coordinates?
column4: This asks whether a very concrete computable symmetry relation represents all countable Borel classification problems.
column5: Define Borel reducibility and the coding of sequences; distinguish full universality from measure universality and from larger finite alphabets.

column3: Is there an infinite computable Polish space such that every two computable presentations of it admit a computable homeomorphism?
column4: This asks whether an infinite complete separable space can have a fully effective topological identity.
column5: Define computable metric presentations, completion, names and computability of homeomorphisms; homeomorphism must not be replaced by isometry.

column3: Does Baire space \(\omega^\omega\) have a least Turing degree relative to which every pair of its computable presentations admits a computable homeomorphism?
column4: A least degree would measure the computational information required to identify arbitrary effective presentations of a basic space.
column5: Define presentation and relative computability of homeomorphisms; existence of a least degree is the main target, with its identification a further source question.

column3: Must every group with a finite confluent length-reducing string-rewriting presentation be a free product of finitely many finite groups and a finitely generated free group?
column4: The conjecture would characterize exactly which group word problems admit this finite normalization mechanism.
column5: Define the presentation alphabet and confluence convention; do not impose inverse-closedness or bounds on right-hand-side lengths absent from the general question.

column3: Is solvability of finite tree equations with ordinary variables and one-hole context variables in \(\mathrm{NP}\)?
column4: This asks for short certificates at the central remaining complexity boundary for context unification.
column5: Specify ranked signatures, sharing and input encoding, and how contexts may repeat; unrestricted instances must not be replaced by well-nested ones.

column3: For each fixed \(k\ge2\), determine the complexity of recognizing false closed prenex CNF quantified Boolean formulas that become true after deletion of any clause, when the number of clauses minus the number of existential variables is \(k\).
column4: The target connects structural deficiency to the difficulty of recognizing minimal inconsistency under quantification.
column5: Specify the formula encoding, deficiency promise, reduction type and required classification; check the distinction between maximal deficiency and raw deficiency in the cited paper.

column3: Can equivalence of two propositional Horn CNF formulas be decided in \(O(N\log N)\) time, where \(N\) is their combined number of literal occurrences?
column4: A near-linear equivalence algorithm would make comparison of entire Horn consequence theories nearly as cheap as reading them.
column5: Specify the machine model and variable encoding; retain linear time as a stronger possible target rather than silently identifying it with the chosen near-linear question.

column3: Do almost-sure termination under every strategy and ordinary local confluence of the lifted multidistribution relation imply a unique limiting distribution on normal forms for probabilistic abstract rewriting?
column4: This asks for a probabilistic counterpart of a fundamental normalization principle.
column5: Define strategies, multidistribution lifting, ordinary local confluence and limit uniqueness; limit-only joinability is explicitly insufficient in the source.

column3: Does the full \(\lambda\sigma\) explicit-substitution calculus admit an effective perpetual reduction strategy, one that produces an infinite reduction whenever the input term admits any infinite reduction?
column4: A perpetual strategy would expose nontermination in a foundational calculus of explicit substitution.
column5: Record the full syntax and rewrite rules, effectiveness model and behavior on normalizing terms; variants of the calculus cannot be substituted.

column3: Can every first-order spectrum be represented by a sentence whose vocabulary contains only one binary relation, preserving the set of finite model sizes exactly?
column4: This asks whether a minimal relational vocabulary suffices to express all finite-model cardinality phenomena.
column5: Specify equality, empty models and spectrum conventions; encodings that change model sizes do not establish the target.

column3: Is there an effectively presented logic defining exactly the finite-structure Boolean queries expressible by order-invariant first-order sentences?
column4: An effective syntax would make semantic order invariance available as a usable formal language.
column5: Specify effective syntax and semantics, vocabularies and compiler requirements; do not assume order invariance itself is decidable.

column3: On every class of finite relational structures with bounded Gaifman degree, is each order-invariant first-order sentence equivalent to an ordinary first-order sentence on that class?
column4: The collapse would show that auxiliary order adds no expressive power in a broad sparse setting.
column5: Specify the fixed degree bound, relational signatures and uniformity of the translation; restricted cluster fragments do not settle the full question.

column3: Is the complement of every language generated by a conjunctive grammar also generated by a conjunctive grammar?
column4: This asks whether grammar conjunction and recursion can express negation without an explicit negation operation.
column5: Define the grammar semantics and complement relative to a fixed alphabet; distinguish the class from Boolean and linear conjunctive grammars.

column3: Can every conjunctive language excluding the empty word be generated by rules \(A\to a\beta_1\mathbin{\&}\cdots\mathbin{\&}a\beta_k\), with each \(\beta_i\) a string of nonterminals?
column4: A Greibach form would impose input-consuming recursion on a broad extension of context-free grammar.
column5: Specify permitted empty nonterminal strings, rule arities and the treatment of the empty language; preserve exact language equivalence.

column3: Given a finite variable pattern \(p\) and an integer \(k\ge2\), is it decidable whether an infinite \(k\)-letter word avoids every nonerasing substitution instance of \(p\)?
column4: This distinguishes decidability with a prescribed alphabet from the easier unrestricted-alphabet existence question.
column5: Specify one-sided versus two-sided infinite words, contiguous occurrence, nonerasing substitutions and encoding of \(k\).

column3: Must every surjective cellular automaton on a full two-sided one-dimensional shift have a dense set of temporally periodic configurations?
column4: The conjecture connects reversible coverage of configurations with recurrence in a basic discrete computation model.
column5: Define the finite alphabet, local rule, product topology and temporal periodicity; do not conflate temporal recurrence with spatial periodicity.

column3: Is there a language recognized by a nondeterministic two-way finite automaton with two input heads that no deterministic two-way finite automaton with two heads recognizes?
column4: This isolates the power of nondeterminism at a fixed number of heads, rather than the state cost of simulation.
column5: Specify endmarkers, head sensing, acceptance and halting conventions; verify the source's precise two-head classes.

column3: Is isomorphism decidable for two promised well-orders presented by finite-tree automata when only their domains and order relations are supplied?
column4: The problem tests whether ordinal structure can be compared algorithmically without an additional automatic addition operation.
column5: Specify injective versus quotient presentations, synchronous tree-automatic relations and how the well-order promise is supplied.

column3: Are languages accepted by one-way deterministic finite-testable multicounter machines with a right endmarker closed under complement?
column4: This asks whether a limited zero-test resource preserves a basic language-theoretic closure property.
column5: Define successful zero-tests, per-counter bounds, acceptance and infinite runs from the cited model.

column3: Is the complement of every language accepted by an unambiguous one-way partially blind multicounter machine accepted by some nondeterministic partially blind multicounter machine?
column4: This isolates the interaction between unambiguity, weak counters and negation.
column5: Specify partially blind counter semantics, endmarkers and acceptance; the output machine is not required to remain unambiguous.

column3: Given a nondeterministic parity automaton on infinite binary trees and a finite priority interval \(J\), is it decidable whether an equivalent nondeterministic automaton using only priorities in \(J\) exists?
column4: The index problem measures how much acceptance complexity is inherently needed to describe a tree language.
column5: Define the parity convention, tree alphabet and equivalence semantics; transformations for deterministic or alternating automata do not settle this model.

column3: Does first-order Gödel logic over truth values \([0,1]\), with function symbols and without built-in equality, have Craig interpolation?
column4: The question asks whether common vocabulary still suffices to explain entailment once functions enter a many-valued logic.
column5: Define semantic consequence and the allowed interpolant vocabulary; distinguish function symbols from the already treated relational case.

column3: Classify the countably infinite closed sets \(V\subseteq[0,1]\) containing \(0,1\) for which an effective transformation sends every first-order formula to a prenex formula preserving validity in Gödel logic over \(V\).
column4: A classification would explain when quantifier normalization remains algorithmically possible in many-valued semantics.
column5: Specify effective dependence on \(V\) and the meaning of classification; preservation of validity is weaker than formula equivalence.

column3: Given an MSO formula \(\varphi(X,Y)\) over the full infinite binary tree, is it decidable whether an MSO-definable function chooses exactly one valid \(Y\) for every \(X\) admitting a witness?
column4: Definable choice connects logical specification to the existence of uniform witnesses.
column5: Specify set-variable arities, the tree signature and functional graph definability; retain unrestricted cross-sections.

column3: Is Church synthesis decidable for Metric Interval Temporal Logic specifications over finitely variable signals on the nonnegative real line, with a causal output operator for every input signal?
column4: The problem asks whether metric real-time specifications can be automatically realized as causal behavior.
column5: Define the exact MITL syntax, interval endpoints, signal conventions and causality at simultaneous events; timed-game variants are not interchangeable.

column3: Can threshold winning probabilities in finite turn-based stochastic parity games be decided in polynomial time when the number of priorities and rational transition probabilities are unrestricted?
column4: This combines randomness, adversarial control and infinite-run specifications in a central quantitative verification task.
column5: Specify threshold comparison, parity convention, player objectives, binary probability encoding and whether exact values or only decisions are required.

column3: Is there a compositional game model of the pure untyped call-by-value lambda calculus whose denotational equality coincides with termination-based contextual equivalence?
column4: Full abstraction would align a structured semantic model exactly with observable program behavior.
column5: Specify the admissible game-model structure so the target is not a trivial contextual quotient; define evaluation and closing contexts.

column3: Does full guarded Kleene algebra with tests admit a finite sound and complete algebraic inference system for guarded-string language equivalence, eliminating the need for an infinitary uniqueness axiom?
column4: A finite axiomatization would give a compact proof theory for structured program equivalence.
column5: Define the full GKAT syntax, allowed inference rules and the infinitary axiom; derivability of one axiom and existence of some finite basis require careful distinction.

column3: Does every proof in Manighetti–Miller's classical fixed-point arithmetic \(\mu\mathrm{LK}_{p}^{+}\) admit a cut-free proof of the same sequent?
column4: Cut elimination would establish a fundamental proof-theoretic property of arithmetic with fixed points.
column5: Transcribe the exact rules for equality, fixed points, weakening and contraction; consistency or arithmetic embedding alone does not imply cut elimination.

column3: Is the monad of all continuous valuations on dcpos commutative, so that the order of two independent probabilistic computations can always be interchanged?
column4: Commutativity determines whether a central denotational model supports unrestricted exchange of probabilistic effects.
column5: Specify the category, valuation mass convention and monad operations; distinguish all continuous valuations from the minimal-valuation submonad.

column3: Given rational \(0<\lambda<1\) and rational \(a,b,t\), is it decidable whether there exists an infinite sequence \(w_i\in\{a,b\}\) satisfying \(\sum_{i\ge0}w_i\lambda^i=t\)?
column4: This elementary-looking arithmetic existence question is a barrier in discounted quantitative verification.
column5: Specify binary rational encoding and all discount factors; this is existence of an exact target sum, not automaton universality or approximate equality.

column3: Is satisfiability decidable for first-order logic with only two variables when one designated binary relation is transitive and other relations are unrestricted, allowing infinite models?
column4: The target isolates a basic boundary between finite-model and unrestricted decidability.
column5: Specify the available relation arities, equality and absence of counting; verify the distinction from finite satisfiability and partial-order restrictions.

column3: Is satisfiability decidable for the equality-free alternating uniform one-dimensional fragment with arbitrary alternation within quantifier blocks?
column4: This asks whether a broad syntactic extension of a decidable logic retains an algorithmic satisfiability boundary.
column5: Define uniformity, allowed blocks and the one-free-variable condition exactly; do not infer the full result from restricted alternation or three-variable fragments.

column3: Can the uniform cut-elimination theorem for \(\mu\mathrm{superLL}^{\infty}\) be extended to digging rules while retaining least and greatest fixed points and validity of nonwellfounded proofs?
column4: The question tests whether one proof-theoretic framework can encompass nested exponential structure as well as recursion.
column5: Recover the precise rule family and validity condition; the source leaves possible restrictions open, so the final mathematical target is not yet fully specified.

column3: Determine the best worst-case expected revenue ratio attainable by a randomized posted price computed from one sample of an unknown monotone-hazard-rate distribution, relative to optimal monopoly revenue for that distribution.
column4: This measures the value of a single observation in a basic truthful pricing problem.
column5: Specify support, atoms, integrability and admissible randomized pricing rules; separate exact ratio identification from the default numerical tolerance.

column3: For independent buyers with subadditive valuations, do fixed anonymous item prices chosen from their known distributions guarantee a universal constant fraction of expected optimal welfare for every arrival order?
column4: This asks whether a simple posted-price interface can match the welfare power of richer allocation mechanisms.
column5: Specify valuation normalization, tie breaking, information available to buyers and whether the arrival adversary sees values or randomness.

column3: Determine the smallest worst-case expected social-cost approximation ratio of a truthful-in-expectation mechanism locating two facilities on the real line without payments.
column4: The sharp ratio would quantify the efficiency cost of truthful location reporting for multiple public facilities.
column5: Specify the agent domain, zero-optimum cases, randomization and admissible output locations; social cost is the sum of distances to the nearer facility.

column3: Can a randomized dominant-strategy truthful-in-expectation combinatorial-auction mechanism achieve a constant fraction of optimal welfare for arbitrary subadditive bidders using polynomial computation and polynomially many demand queries?
column4: This targets the welfare attainable from strategic bidders with broad complement-free preferences.
column5: Define demand-query precision, payments, feasibility and computation costs; this differs from universal truthfulness for submodular bidders in the existing catalogue.

column3: In undirected network-design games with arbitrary terminal pairs and equal sharing of each used edge's cost, is the minimum-cost pure Nash equilibrium within a universal constant factor of the socially optimal network?
column4: The price of stability asks how much inefficiency is unavoidable even in the best stable outcome.
column5: Specify feasible paths, nonnegative edge costs, player deviations and the comparison optimum; single-source games are a restricted case.

column3: For every number of teams, is there a monotone Condorcet-consistent randomized tournament rule satisfying the source's two-team nonmanipulability condition with selfishness parameter one?
column4: A sharp incentive threshold would identify how much internal sacrifice is needed to prevent collusion in tournament selection.
column5: Write the exact inequalities defining the selfishness parameter and monotonicity; the informal probability-sacrifice description is not a complete model.

column3: Can a polynomial-query black-box transformation turn any allocation algorithm under independent known single-parameter value distributions into a dominant-strategy truthful-in-expectation mechanism preserving its expected welfare?
column4: This asks whether algorithmic welfare can be retained when incentives are strengthened beyond Bayesian truthfulness.
column5: Specify access to priors, feasibility information, output payments and the meaning of exact welfare preservation; stronger black-box impossibilities may concern a different target.

column3: Determine the optimal worst-case approximation ratio of randomized truthful-in-expectation mechanisms for two-way kidney exchange with arbitrarily many hospitals that may hide vertices and internally match their remaining patients.
column4: The ratio quantifies the welfare cost of strategic participation by institutions in exchange networks.
column5: Define hospital utilities, allowed internal matching and deviations, zero-optimum cases and the mechanism's information; preserve the unrestricted hospital count.

column3: Does ordinary Learning With Errors hardness alone imply witness encryption for every NP relation, with witness-based decryption and indistinguishability of messages on false public instances?
column4: This asks for the minimal assumptions needed to encrypt against the existence of mathematical witnesses.
column5: Specify LWE parameters and hardness, uniformity and the witness-encryption security game; evasive LWE or obfuscation assumptions are not ordinary LWE.

column3: Does the existence of one-way functions imply a dual pseudorandom function, remaining pseudorandom after exchanging the roles of key and input?
column4: Dual pseudorandomness tests how much symmetric cryptographic structure follows from the weakest standard hardness primitive.
column5: Specify domains, matching key/input lengths, adaptive security and reductions; distinguish arbitrary one-way functions from permutations.

column3: Does ordinary LWE alone imply public-key functional encryption for arbitrary polynomial-size circuits secure against polynomially many colluding functional-key holders?
column4: This asks whether a central lattice assumption supports general fine-grained access to encrypted data.
column5: Specify selective versus adaptive security, simulation versus indistinguishability, admissible key queries and LWE parameters; bounded collusion is weaker.

column3: Are there explicit polynomial-time encodable and decodable information-theoretic nonmalleable codes for independent tampering of two shares, with negligible error and rate approaching \(1/2\)?
column4: This asks whether efficient split-state coding can reach its information-theoretic capacity.
column5: Define the nonmalleability experiment, rate convention, security parameter and uniform approach to capacity; preserve independent tampering of exactly two shares.

column3: Do one-way functions imply fully adaptively secure publicly verifiable random functions on exponentially large domains in the standard model?
column4: The question tests whether public verifiability requires stronger assumptions than ordinary private pseudorandomness.
column5: Define uniqueness, correctness and pseudorandomness games, domain growth and uniformity; black-box separations do not refute unrestricted constructions.

column3: Can DDH yield two-party one-private additive homomorphic secret sharing for arbitrary polynomial-size circuits, with output-share size independent of the evaluated circuit?
column4: This asks whether general secure evaluation can be supported under a substantially different assumption from those used for full homomorphic encryption.
column5: Specify the group family, circuit-output algebra, privacy game, setup and compactness parameters; retain the source's editorial DDH specialization.

column3: Does LWE alone yield constant-round plain-model zero-knowledge arguments for all NP languages under arbitrary polynomially many interleaved sessions, with polynomial-time simulation?
column4: The target combines minimal assumptions, concurrency and a constant interaction cost.
column5: Specify uniform simulation, adversarial scheduling, auxiliary input and LWE parameters; bounded-player or superpolynomial-simulation variants do not meet this target.

column3: Does ordinary LWE imply noninteractive succinct arguments for all NP relations in the common-reference-string model, with proof size \(\mathrm{poly}(\lambda,\log T)\) and verification time \(\mathrm{poly}(\lambda,|x|,\log T)\) for \(T\)-step witness verification?
column4: This asks whether one standard assumption suffices for very short general computational proofs.
column5: Specify setup, completeness, adaptive soundness, prover complexity and LWE parameters; exclude additional random-oracle, knowledge and proof-complexity assumptions.

column3: Can single-server private information retrieval achieve \(N\operatorname{polylog}N\) server preprocessing time and storage together with polylogarithmic online query time and communication under Ring LWE, with only small client state?
column4: The question asks whether privacy-preserving database access can have almost optimal preparation as well as fast queries.
column5: Separate security-parameter factors from \(N\), specify client state and query costs, and require server-only preprocessing independent of a client.

column3: Does the existence of one-way functions imply classical plain-model blind signatures with blindness and one-more unforgeability, allowing polynomially many rounds and non-black-box techniques?
column4: This asks how little computational hardness suffices for anonymous authenticated transactions.
column5: Specify concurrent signing interactions and exact security games; neither black-box impossibility nor a construction using a global random oracle settles the target.

column3: Determine the infimum asymptotic competitive ratio of deterministic online bin packing with irrevocable placement in unit-capacity bins.
column4: The constant measures the irreducible loss caused by committing to packing decisions without future items.
column5: Define input sizes, allowed item values and the uniform additive constant; distinguish asymptotic from absolute competitiveness.

column3: Determine the smallest worst-case stretch of deterministic online packing into \(m\) bins when the full sequence is promised to fit offline into \(m\) unit-capacity bins, in the regime of arbitrarily large \(m\).
column4: This measures how much extra capacity is needed when the number of bins is fixed but item order is online.
column5: Specify whether the target is a supremum or a limiting value over \(m\), item range and additive conventions; the former three-halves threshold is already surpassed.

column3: Determine the optimal deterministic competitive ratio for single-machine total completion time when all jobs are initially present, each has a known test duration, and its processing time is revealed only after its mandatory nonpreemptive test.
column4: The problem quantifies the cost of acquiring information before scheduling work.
column5: Specify zero durations, separation of test and execution, offline benchmark and input encoding; the target allows unequal test durations.

column3: Determine the optimal randomized competitive ratio against an oblivious adversary for single-machine total completion time when every initially present job needs a mandatory unit-time test revealing its processing time.
column4: This isolates the value of randomization in scheduling with compulsory information acquisition.
column5: Specify nonpreemptive test and processing operations, expected-cost ratio and the offline benchmark, which must also test every job.

column3: Is there a deterministic three-competitive file-migration algorithm on every metric space when serving a request costs its distance from the file and moving the file costs \(D\) times the distance moved?
column4: The target asks whether a canonical state-location problem reaches its known lower-bound ratio.
column5: Specify admissible \(D\), initial location, service/migration order and additive competitiveness; the title should reflect the three-competitive proposition.

column3: Determine the largest universal factor \(\alpha\) achievable by selecting at most one of independent nonnegative values from known distributions arriving in uniformly random order, relative to their expected maximum.
column4: The prophet-secretary constant quantifies the value of distribution knowledge under random arrival.
column5: Specify whether identities are observed, integrability, randomization, atoms and tie breaking; an unattained supremum needs approaching guarantees.

column3: Is there a polynomial-time constant-factor approximation for preemptive single-machine scheduling with release times and arbitrary nonnegative nondecreasing job-specific completion-cost functions?
column4: A constant approximation would unify many completion-time objectives under one general scheduling model.
column5: Specify finite representations or oracle access to cost functions, processing-time encodings and approximation conventions; quasipolynomial time does not settle the stated target.

column3: Characterize finite policy classes \(\Pi\) that permit learning an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal member in every unknown horizon-\(H\) MDP using \(\mathrm{poly}(H,\log|\Pi|,1/\varepsilon)\) online episodes, for a fixed finite action set.
column4: A structural characterization would distinguish statistically tractable online reinforcement learning from settings needing stronger access.
column5: Specify rewards, state spaces, policy encoding, confidence and the form of a necessary-and-sufficient condition; a generative model changes the problem.

column3: Can a Poisson binomial distribution on \(n\) Bernoulli summands be properly learned from samples to total-variation error \(\varepsilon\) in time polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\) and \(\log n\), using a compressed representation of distinct parameters and multiplicities?
column4: This asks whether the structural requirement on the output imposes more than polynomial learning cost.
column5: Specify confidence, sample complexity, parameter precision and output size; recovering the original summands is not required.

column3: If an automatic language family is identifiable in the limit from positive data by an automatic learner with unrestricted memory, is it also learnable with memory length at most the longest example seen plus a constant?
column4: This asks whether extra memory genuinely increases the power of finite-state-style learning.
column5: Define automatic families and learners, legal hypothesis recodings and success on all texts; negative counterexamples are not available.

column3: Does hypothesis-length-bounded auxiliary memory strictly increase the automatic language families learnable in the limit from positive data beyond automatic iterative learning?
column4: The comparison isolates the informational power of auxiliary memory in constrained learning models.
column5: Specify automatic transitions, memory accounting and permitted hypothesis-space recodings; fixed restrictive indexings could change the answer.

column3: Can a minimum-total-Euclidean-length perfect red-blue matching of \(n\) red and \(n\) blue planar points with arbitrary real coordinates be computed in \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) time for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\)?
column4: The question tests whether exact geometric bipartite optimization can break the quadratic barrier.
column5: Specify the exact real-arithmetic primitives and deterministic versus randomized time; the existing unrestricted planar matching card explicitly excludes a merely bipartite result.

column3: Determine the optimal worst-case size of a \((t,\varepsilon)\)-approximate Voronoi diagram for \(n\) sites in fixed-dimensional Euclidean space, using quadtree boxes or differences of boxes with at most \(t\) representative sites per cell.
column4: The tradeoff quantifies the geometric storage needed to reduce approximate nearest-neighbor queries to a small candidate set.
column5: Define the subdivision model and size measure, parameter ranges and scale normalization; this is not the unrestricted nearest-neighbor data-structure problem.

column3: Does every directed planar graph with nonnegative weights admit an exact distance oracle with \(O(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) space, polylogarithmic query time and polynomial preprocessing?
column4: This asks whether planarity permits simultaneously compact and fast exact distance queries.
column5: Specify machine and weight representation, randomization, disconnected pairs and preprocessing dependence; approximate undirected oracles are different targets.

column3: For every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), can a one-pass algorithm produce a \((1-\varepsilon)\)-approximate maximum matching using \(O_{\varepsilon}(n\operatorname{polylog}n)\) space when edges arrive in uniformly random order?
column4: The target asks how much random order can improve a severe streaming-memory constraint.
column5: Specify success probability, simple versus multigraph inputs and output matching storage; do not transfer adversarial-order impossibility to this model.

column3: For every undirected capacitated graph with \(k\) terminals and every \(\varepsilon>0\), is there a graph of size \(f(k,\varepsilon)\), independent of the original graph and capacities, preserving all terminal multicommodity-flow congestion values within \(1+\varepsilon\)?
column4: This tests whether terminal flow behavior admits an arbitrarily accurate finite summary independent of the original network.
column5: Define the demands, congestion convention and size measure; allow new nonterminals and do not restrict the sparsifier to a contraction.
